newsitem.title: UK: UK ex-minister quits as Queen's adviser - reports.
newsitem.headline: UK ex-minister quits as Queen's adviser - reports.

text.p: Disgraced former cabinet minister Jonathan Aitken has quit as a confidential adviser to Queen Elizabeth just days after dropping a libel action over sleaze allegations, British press reports said on Wednesday.
A Cabinet Office spokeswoman said she could not confirm that Aitken had become only the third member of the Privy Council this century to resign.
"We have received a letter from Mr Aitken, but I cannot comment on its contents," she said, adding that a meeting of the Council would take place later this week.

Aitken, who was number two at the Treasury in 1994-95, dropped his libel action against the Guardian newspaper and Granada television last week after defence lawyers said they had uncovered new evidence casting doubt on his case.

The 54-year-old sued over allegations made in 1995 that he was financially dependent on wealthy Saudi business associates, procured prostitutes for them, and tried to arrange arms sales to Iraq at the height of the Iran-Iraq war.
He also denied allowing a Saudi associate to pay for a stay at the luxurious Ritz hotel in Paris while a minister and later lying to civil servants about the matter.
Police are now investigating allegations of perjury and of seeking to pervert the course of justice against Aitken, whose marriage break-up was announced on the eve of the libel case being withdrawn.
Aitken, currently believed to be in the United States, lost his seat in parliament in last month's general election.
He automatically became a member of the Privy Council when he joined then Prime Minister John Major's cabinet three years ago.

Membership of the prestigious body, which includes top judges and church dignitaries as well as senior politicians from all parties, is usually for life. Members can call themselves "The Right Honourable".
Only three members have previously left or been forced out of the body this century.
Ex-ministers John Profumo, who lied to parliament about a relationship with a prostitute in the 1960s, and John Stonehouse, who faked his own death in an insurance scam in 1976, both resigned.
Edgar Speyer was thrown out in 1921 after being found guilty of collaborating with Germany in World War One.
